catalog_quote: Stress There is very little textual evidence as to how Cornish was stressed. Evidence from place-names suggests that the pattern was the same as in Breton (though not the Gwenedeg dialect thereof). We may surmise that, in common with Breton and Welsh, the normal stress in polysyllables was originally on the ultimate syllable, and that it changed, perhaps c. 1050, to the penultimate. Unpublished work by Keith Bailey on stress in Middle Cornish verse suggests that, as in Welsh, the stress-accent was usually on the penultimate syllable, but the pitch-accent remained on the ultimate. ... [p. 507] Normal stress in polysyllables The primary stress fell on the penultimate syllable, and a secondary stress fell on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end. This applied to most polysyllables, including close compounds. ... [Table 11.6, p. 498, 'Major developments in the phonological history of Cornish': Phase PrimC > OldC ... Development: shift of accent; Date: c. 1050; Did this happen in Breton? partially; Welsh? yes]

new_statements.rule_in_words: Reconstructed, not observed: in Primitive and Old Cornish (the SW British stage) word stress in polysyllables fell on the final syllable (the old British penult, made final by 6th-c. apocope); c. 1050 (Jackson: 11th century; George Table 11.6 'shift of accent c. 1050') it retracted to the penultimate, so only the very end of the Old Cornish period (Vocabularium Cornicum, c. 1100) and all later Cornish had regular penultimate stress. Toorians 2014 (from George 1984 PHC 7.5.5) states the same: 'Until ca. 1050 accent on the last syllable.'
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing stated for the pre-shift (final-stress) stage. For post-shift Cornish George (p. 507) gives primary stress on the penult and 'a secondary stress.. on the fourth and sixth syllables from the end'; he and Toorians (n. 4, after Watkins) add that the pitch accent may have remained on the ultimate after the stress moved to the penult.
new_statements.exceptions: None for the Old Cornish stage. Post-shift (Middle Cornish) exceptions listed p. 507: unstressed article/possessives/particles/conjunctions/prepositions; double stress (second primary) in loose compounds, noun+adjective and Pen-zance-type place-names; antepenultimate stress in 3+-syllable words with an epenthetic vowel (banathel) and some English loans; final stress in shortened forms (yma, verbs in -he), many adverbs/prepositions (ynweth, avel), compounds of war-/na-, some English loans (attes).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress of polysyllables, inferred from comparative Brittonic evidence and place-names ('very little textual evidence'); the languoid is a historical stage (c. 600/800-1200) during which the position changed (final -> penultimate c. 1050), and the absolute date of the shift is disputed for Brittonic generally (Jackson 11th c; Watkins/McCone 9th c. for Welsh, per Willis 2009: 122-123). Reading 'fixed: final syllable' describes the stage before c. 1050; for the last century of Old Cornish the reading would be fixed: penultimate syllable.
new_statements.identity_note: Glottolog 'Old South-West British' [oldc1252] carries ISO 639-3 oco = Old Cornish, the stage of Cornish c. 800-1200 (Bodmin manumissions, glosses, Saints' List, Vocabularium Cornicum c. 1100) descending from Jackson's 'South-West British' dialect of Late British, and scarcely distinct from Old Breton before c. 1100. George 2009 describes 'Traditional Cornish' (600-1800) as a whole with explicit Primitive/Old/Middle/Late phases; the quoted stress passage is a diachronic reconstruction: final stress in Primitive and Old Cornish until c. 1050, penultimate thereafter (= Middle/Late Cornish, corn1251, already catalogued separately). The same shift is shared by Welsh and by Breton except Gwenedeg/Vannetais (final stress). No source describes stress from Old Cornish textual data directly ('very little textual evidence').

sources.note: Very little textual evidence; place-names suggest the Breton (non-Gwenedeg) pattern; stress in polysyllables was originally on the ultimate and changed 'perhaps c. 1050' to the penultimate (Table 11.6: PrimC>OldC 'shift of accent c. 1050', shared 'partially' by Breton, by Welsh); after the shift primary stress penultimate, secondary on 4th/6th syllable from end, pitch accent possibly still on the ultimate (Bailey, unpublished); lists MC exceptions (double stress in loose compounds, antepenult with epenthetic vowels, final stress in shortened forms/adverbs/loans).

Second-hand: stress in polysyllables originally final in the earliest Cornish (citing Jackson 1953:265; Schrijver 1995), shifted to the penult in the eleventh century (Jackson 1953:682-9); George 2009a:506 for monosyllables and pitch accent.

sources.note: MC stress normally penultimate as in Welsh and most Breton (citing George PHC 5.3.2, 6.2.7); ch. 13: 'Until ca. 1050 accent on the last syllable (PHC 7.5.5). With the accent shift started the reduction of vowels in final syllables.' n.4 summarises Watkins: main accent in OW 'and probably in the other Brittonic languages' a pitch accent on the ultimate; Jackson's 11th-c. 'accent shift' = concentration of stress on the penult. Second-hand from George 1984.
